analysis.one_liner: Freezes new permits for plastics plants, tightens their pollution rules, and cuts single-use plastics.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in April 2024 and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025, with support from 7 senators and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Environmental Protection Agency to treat plastic production as a pollution problem across its whole life cycle. It would put a hold on new permits for plastics and petrochemical plants until stronger air and water rules take effect, require plants to monitor and limit their emissions, force companies to report the chemicals they use, cut single-use plastic packaging by at least 25% by 2034, and require that residents living next to these plants get advance notice, hearings, and a say before permits are approved. It would also list discarded PVC plastic as hazardous waste and ban new plants within 5 miles of schools, homes, parks, and similar places.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near plastics and petrochemical plants — disproportionately low-income communities and communities of color — would get stricter emissions limits, real-time pollution monitoring, advance notice of permitting decisions, and formal consultation. Broader benefits would flow to the public through reduced single-use plastic pollution, cleaner air and water, and new federal study of microplastics in food.

how_it_helps.text: Places a moratorium on new air and water permits for plastics and petrochemical facilities until the bill's new pollution standards are in effect, and bars export of raw plastic feedstocks during that pause.

Requires new federal emissions standards for plastics plants within 3 years, limits flaring to safety emergencies only, and mandates continuous, publicly available monitoring of benzene and other hazardous pollutants.

Requires a near-zero (0 milligrams per liter) discharge limit for priority pollutants and plastic pellets from plastics plants, and requires permits to account for cumulative pollution already burdening an area.

Requires environmental justice assessments before plastics-plant permits are approved, with direct notification to nearby residents, public hearings with translation services, a 45-day waiting period, and community benefit agreements as a permit condition.

Requires EPA to list discarded PVC as hazardous waste, prioritize styrene and vinyl chloride for regulation, and conduct a cumulative public-health assessment of plants' combined chemical exposures on nearby communities and workers.

Sets federal targets to cut single-use plastic packaging by at least 25% by 2034 and shift at least 30% of packaging to reusable and refillable systems by 2034, with a grant program prioritizing low-income communities and communities of color.
Prohibits new plastics facilities from being sited within 5 miles of a school, residence, daycare, nursing home, hospital, park, or similar community space.

analysis.who_pays: Petrochemical and plastics manufacturers would bear the main costs: a permit freeze on new and expanded plants, stricter emission and wastewater rules, mandatory monitoring, financial assurance for cleanup, a 5-mile siting exclusion, and disclosure of the chemicals they use. Beverage and consumer goods companies would face mandates to reduce single-use packaging. Oil and gas companies would lose projected demand growth from plastics. Some costs could reach consumers through higher packaging and product prices.

drawbacks.text: The permit moratorium would stop new and expanded plastics plants indefinitely — until the EPA finalizes a long list of rules — which could delay capacity for everyday plastic goods and shift production overseas rather than reducing it globally.

The 5-mile siting ban and near-zero discharge limits would sharply restrict where plastics plants can operate and how, raising industry compliance costs that could be passed to consumers through higher prices.
The bill bans export of covered petrochemical products during the pause period, a trade restriction affecting a major export sector.
The reuse and refill targets would require a wholesale redesign of food and beverage packaging systems on a short timeline, with unknown costs and logistical challenges for small businesses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections for fenceline communities — monitoring, cumulative-impact analysis, and a real voice in permitting — are substantial and directly target documented health burdens from pollution. The costs are real but are concentrated on an industry whose growth projections depend on expanding production near those same communities; the pause's open-ended duration and the export ban are the provisions most open to fair objection, since they could disrupt supply and shift production abroad rather than shrink global plastics output.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in April 2024, and no one on the committee — where the same party held the majority — ever scheduled it for consideration or a vote, and the Congress ended in January 2025 with the bill dead.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill in the Senate on April 18, 2024, joined by five Democratic senators and one independent.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day it was introduced.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never considered the bill, no vote occurred in either chamber, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill attracted six cosponsors — five Democrats and one independent — and no Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Petrochemical and plastics producers are better off, since the permit freeze, tighter emission standards, hazardous-waste listing for PVC, and siting restrictions never took effect. Beverage and consumer goods companies are also spared the packaging reduction and reuse mandates, while communities near plants saw no new protections.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and set out a permitting freeze, emission standards, and community-consultation requirements for plastics facilities.

for.name: 5 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Merkley, Van Hollen, Sanders, Durbin, Markey).

against.name: Tom Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration or a markup in the nine months between referral and the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or allied independents, and no Republican ever signed on; no vote was ever taken, so no party breakdown exists beyond the sponsorship list.

industries.note: The bill would freeze permits for new and expanded plants, impose new air and water pollution standards, mandate continuous monitoring, require community benefit agreements, and bar plants within 5 miles of schools and homes. Its provisions target an industry whose projected growth depends on siting facilities next to low-income communities and communities of color, where those same costs fall today.

The bill is built around the finding that plastics are forecast to become the largest driver of oil and gas demand by 2050, and it would restrict permits and exports of ethylene, propylene, and raw plastic feedstocks during the pause period, cutting into projected demand growth.

industries.industry: Beverage and consumer packaged goods companies
industries.note: Producers of single-use plastic packaging and food service products would face federal targets to cut single-use packaging by at least 25% by 2034 and shift 30% to reusable and refillable systems, plus reporting obligations. Consumers might share the cost through prices, but the current system externalizes pollution onto nearby communities.

The bill classifies pyrolysis, gasification, and incineration facilities as covered facilities subject to the permitting freeze and bars EPA from counting them as recycling, directly blocking a sector that markets itself as the plastics-waste solution.

The bill would require EPA to list discarded PVC as hazardous waste and to prioritize styrene and vinyl chloride for regulation under the toxic substances law — the strongest single provision aimed at one plastics product line.
